t.E320.agn: In its 2011 re-evaluation, EFSA stated that BHA does not raise a concern for genotoxicity; it considered that forestomach tumours in rats (an organ with no counterpart in humans) may no longer be relevant for human risk assessment. Based on growth retardation and behavioural effects in young rats, it raised the ADI to 1.0 mg/kg body weight (0.5 in 1989) and stated that estimated intake at current use levels is generally below this limit. IARC, for its part, stated in 1986 that there was sufficient evidence for forestomach tumours in animals and no data in humans, and in 1987 classified BHA in Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans).
t.E320.body: BHA is absorbed from the intestine; in the liver it is conjugated with glucuronic acid or sulphate and excreted in the urine. There is evidence that at very high doses it can accumulate in fatty tissue; no accumulation has been seen in other tissues.
t.E320.eff.0.t: IARC classified it in Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) on the basis of forestomach tumours in animals; in 2011 EFSA stated that these tumours may not be relevant to humans and that there is no genotoxicity concern
t.E320.eval: Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic) according to IARC. In 2011 EFSA set the acceptable daily intake at 1 mg/kg. In the EU its use is subject to level limits; it may be found in frying oils, powdered soups and seasonings.
t.E320.found.0: Frying oils and industrial cooking fats
t.E320.prod: Produced chemically by reacting 4-hydroxyanisole with isobutylene (or from hydroquinone).
t.E320.regx.0: Re-evaluated; ADI 1.0 mg/kg body weight/day (raised from the previous 0.5). Intake at current uses is generally below the ADI.
t.E320.regx.1: Authorised with maximum levels in specific categories (e.g. 200 mg/kg on a fat basis in powdered soups and seasonings).
t.E320.summary: A petroleum-derived synthetic antioxidant. It delays rancidity in fats, chewing gum and cereal products.
t.E320.what: It is a synthetic antioxidant that delays fats spoiling with oxygen and going rancid.
